problems.stem: A designer writes: "I moved the Continue button to the bottom-right because that looks more modern." What turns this into a defensible LXD decision rather than a taste call?
options: Keep the rationale but add that several colleagues agreed it looked better.
Name the learner constraint (novices scanned past the button when it floated mid-frame) and the evidence (3 of 5 pilot users missed it) that the move resolves.
Replace the button with an animated arrow so the frame feels livelier.
Cite a recent design-trend article that recommends bottom-right placement.
problems.explanation: LXD as a decision discipline means a choice is justified by a named learner constraint and inspectable evidence, not by appearance or popularity.

problems.stem: In what order should a learning designer settle a storyboard frame so the result is a decision and not a stack of features?
options: Feature first, then media, then purpose, so the tool capabilities lead.
Purpose first (what the learner should be able to do), media choice second, software feature last.
Media first, then purpose, then feature, because the medium is the message.
All three at once, since they are equally important.
problems.explanation: Purpose-first sequencing keeps the feature accountable to a learner action instead of reverse-justifying a feature you already added.

problems.stem: Two storyboard drafts are identical except the second one cites cognitive load theory in its rationale note. What is the problem with the second draft?
options: Citing theory in a rationale note is always inappropriate for a storyboard.
The anchor is named but changed nothing in the frame, so it is decoration, not design reasoning.
Cognitive load theory cannot apply to storyboards, only to finished software.
The second draft is stronger because it references a peer-reviewed source.
problems.explanation: An anchor counts as evidence of judgment only when it alters a concrete element. Identical frames with a citation show name-dropping, not reasoning.

problems.stem: A reviewer says your storyboard "reads like there was only ever one option." Which addition best repairs the design memo?
options: A longer paragraph praising the chosen frame.
A rejected alternative (single-column narration) and the constraint that ruled it out (it doubled reading time for the slowest learners).
A second polished mockup of the same chosen frame.
A note that the deadline left no time for alternatives.
problems.explanation: A decision implies a road not taken. Recording the rejected option and the constraint that eliminated it lets a reviewer audit the trade-off.
